summary: Defines Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers, which shorten the gap when a mobile node moves from one access router to another. During that gap the node cannot send or receive packets because of link-switching delay and IP protocol operations.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move between Wi-Fi spots, you can lose connection for a moment. This note sets up the next spot ahead of time, so the break is shorter.

questions: how to reduce handover delay in mobile ipv6
what is fast handover in mobile ipv6
what is the difference between predictive and reactive fast handover
what does the fast binding update do
how does fmipv6 secure the fast binding update
subtitle: How a roaming IPv6 device sets up its next router in advance so traffic barely pauses when it moves.

tldr.problem: When a Mobile IPv6 node moves to a new access router, it cannot send or receive packets while it detects the move, configures a new address and updates its bindings. This handover latency is often unacceptable for real-time traffic such as VoIP.
tldr.mechanism: The node learns about the next router and builds its new Care-of Address while still on the old link. The old router then tunnels packets to the new address, and the node announces itself on the new link with an Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement as soon as it attaches.
tldr.outcome: The protocol shortens the IP-layer part of handover. It does not improve link-switching delay, it is meant for deployments where address collisions are very unlikely, and it needs a security association between the node and its old router.

today: RFC 5568 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2009. It obsoletes RFC 5268 and has been updated by RFC 7411; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5568 defines Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers. Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) lets a mobile node keep its Internet connectivity as it moves from one access router to another. The combined cost of link-layer procedures, movement detection, IP address configuration and location update is often large enough to hurt real-time applications. Throughput-sensitive applications can benefit from a shorter gap too.

The specification tackles two problems: how a mobile node can send packets as soon as it detects a new subnet link, and how packets can be delivered to it as soon as the new access router detects its attachment. It defines IP messages that work regardless of link technology, while allowing link-specific customizations.

Its limits are stated plainly. It does not improve link-switching latency, does not change how the node signals its home agent, and does not handle bulk movement of nodes using aggregate prefixes. It is aimed at Mobile IPv6 but could be used with any mechanism that lets communication continue despite movement.

This document also replaces RFC 5268. Handover Initiate (HI) and Handover Acknowledge (HAck) now travel in the Mobility Header instead of ICMPv6, and implementations MUST NOT send the old ICMPv6 forms.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving between networks leaves a short gap with no connection. This document is a plan to make that gap much smaller by getting ready before the move.

sections.title: Terminology and Roles
sections.content:
The reference scenario has a Mobile Node (MN), a Previous Access Router (PAR) that is its default router before the move, and a New Access Router (NAR) that is its expected default router afterwards. A Care-of Address (CoA) is the address valid on a router's subnet: the Previous CoA (PCoA) on the PAR's subnet and the New CoA (NCoA) on the NAR's subnet.

An Access Point (AP) is a Layer 2 device that gives the MN wireless connectivity, and its AP-ID is its L2 address. The pair of an AP-ID and the router information behind it is called an [AP-ID, AR-Info] tuple, where AR-Info is the router's L2 address, its IP address and its prefix.

Two modes are named. In predictive fast handover the MN sends its Fast Binding Update while still attached to the PAR, so forwarding starts before it reaches the NAR. In reactive fast handover the MN can send it only after attaching to the NAR. In assigned addressing, the NAR itself picks the NCoA for the MN.
sections.plainLanguage: There is the place you are leaving (the old router), the place you are going to (the new router), and a home address that follows you. Each place gives you a temporary address, like a locker number.

sections.title: How a Fast Handover Works
sections.content:
The protocol attacks three delays. To cut movement detection and new address configuration, the MN sends a Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr) to its current router. The router answers with a Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) that carries [AP-ID, AR-Info] tuples. With that, the MN can build a prospective NCoA before it leaves. These two messages set up no state at the access router.

To cut Binding Update latency, the MN sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to the PAR, asking it to bind the PCoA to the NCoA. The PAR then tunnels packets arriving for the PCoA to the NCoA, and the MN SHOULD reverse tunnel its own packets to the PAR so that a PCoA source address is not dropped by ingress filtering. The tunnel stays up until the MN finishes its Binding Updates with its correspondents.

Finally, the MN announces itself on the new link with an Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement (UNA, with the O bit cleared). Normal address resolution on the NAR can take multiple seconds because retransmissions are by default one second apart, so the UNA lets the NAR forward packets right away.

The access routers also exchange Handover Initiate (HI) and Handover Acknowledge (HAck) messages. These confirm that the proposed NCoA is acceptable, allow the NAR to assign a different one, and request buffering. Both messages SHOULD be used.

If the MN received the Fast Binding Acknowledgment (FBack) on the old link, tunneling is already running when it arrives. If it did not, it sends the UNA first and then sends the FBU again. In some wireless technologies the network decides when to hand over; then the PAR can send an unsolicited PrRtAdv, and the MN MUST process it and send an FBU to the PAR before switching links.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you move, you ask your old router what the new place looks like and pick your new locker number. Your old router starts forwarding your mail there. When you arrive you shout hello, and the mail is handed to you at once.

sections.title: Protocol Details
sections.content:
The PAR answers an RtSolPr in one of several ways. If it does not know the new access point, it says so and the MN MUST stop fast handover operations on that link. If the access point hangs off the same interface, no further action is needed. If it is known, the PAR supplies the tuple, or indicates that the access point does not support fast handover. A wildcard asks for the neighborhood's tuples, limited by the link MTU.

On an FBU, the PAR SHOULD send an HI to the NAR before creating the binding, and can find the NAR by a longest prefix match of the NCoA against its list of neighboring routers. HI uses Code 0 when the FBU came from the PAR's link (source address is the PCoA) and Code 1 when it came from the NAR's link.

For HI with Code 0 the NAR checks that the NCoA is unique by sending a Duplicate Address Detection probe, then proxies the address for PROXY_ND_LIFETIME while it waits for the MN. With assigned addressing it allocates the NCoA itself. If it cannot accept an NCoA it MAY create a host route for the PCoA and set up a reverse tunnel to the PAR. In every case it answers with a HAck. For Code 1 the NAR MUST skip these steps and relies on its trust in the PAR.

If the HAck carries an assigned NCoA, the FBack MUST include it and the MN MUST use it. If the MN gets no FBack after retransmitting the FBU for FBU_RETRIES, it assumes fast handover is not available and stops.

On attaching to the NAR the MN sends the UNA, sends an FBU after it if no FBack arrived, joins the all-nodes and solicited-node multicast groups, and starts its own DAD probe for the NCoA. When the NAR receives the UNA it removes its proxy entry, marks the neighbor cache entry STALE, and forwards arriving and buffered packets. If the NAR prefers a different address, it MAY send a Router Advertisement with the NAACK option, and the MN MUST use the address given.
sections.plainLanguage: Your old router checks with the new one that your chosen locker is free. If it is not, the new router hands you a different one, and you must use that.

sections.title: Buffering, DAD and Fast Movement
sections.content:
Packet loss. Packets can reach the NAR before the MN has linked up, or reach the PAR before the FBU is processed. They are lost unless buffered. HI can request buffering at the NAR, and a PAR asking for that SHOULD provide its own buffering. Draining a buffer too fast can itself cause loss, so routers MUST implement at least a default algorithm based on the original arrival rates: a maximum of 5 packets MAY be sent back to back, and later packets SHOULD be paced by metering the rate at which packets entered the buffer. The RFC calls this default crude.

Duplicate Address Detection. DAD adds delay, so the protocol SHOULD only be used where address collisions are extremely unlikely or not a concern. The delay can be turned off by setting DupAddrDetectTransmits to zero on the NAR. A NAR may also keep a pool of duplicate-free addresses and report that in HAck or NAACK.

Fast or erroneous movement. Moving faster than bindings can be updated (a few seconds) may cause packet loss. An MN returning to the PAR before updating its bindings MUST send an FBU with the Home Address equal to its PCoA and a lifetime of zero, so the PAR can end the temporary tunnel. Such tunnels should have short lifetimes, of the order of tens of seconds. An MN that finds itself on an unanticipated router SHOULD send a new FBU, which supersedes the old binding.

sections.plainLanguage: If mail arrives before you do, someone holds it in a box. They should hand it over a few at a time, not dump it all on you at once.

sections.title: Messages and Options
sections.content:
RtSolPr and PrRtAdv are ICMPv6 messages of Type 154, told apart by a Subtype field: 2 for RtSolPr and 3 for PrRtAdv. HI and HAck are Mobility Header messages, as are the FBU (Mobility Header type 8) and FBack (type 9). The FBU has the same format as a Mobile IPv6 Binding Update, and the FBack the same as a Binding Acknowledgment, but with slightly different processing rules.

The FBU MUST set the A and H flags, MUST carry the Home Address option set to the PCoA, and MUST carry an alternate CoA option set to the NCoA when sent from the PAR's link. HAck codes below 128 mean the handover was accepted; 128 and above mean it was refused. FBack status values below 128 mean the FBU was accepted, and 128 to 131 are rejections.

The new options include an IP Address/Prefix option (type 17) and a Link-Layer Address option (type 19), plus Mobility Header variants of both. The NAACK option (type 20) tells the MN to use a different NCoA, and its status codes include 4, which means a PCoA was supplied and no FBU should be sent. The BADF option (type 21) MUST be present in the FBU and FBack and MUST be the last Mobility Option. By default the MAC is HMAC_SHA1 with the first 96 bits used, and other algorithms such as HMAC_SHA256 can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a form with boxes to fill in and a code number saying what it means. There is also a signature box so the receiver knows the form is not fake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An unprotected FBU would let an attacker steal or redirect packets for someone else's address. So the PAR MUST ensure the FBU came from a node that legitimately owns the PCoA. The FBU and FBack carry the BADF option, computed from a shared handover key. That key comes from a companion protocol, RFC 5269.

Even a correctly secured FBU could point at an unsuspecting node by mistake or on purpose. The PAR MUST verify that the NCoA belongs to the NAR's prefix, using HI and HAck. The NAR proxies the NCoA so that nothing reaches the link until the MN attaches and sends its UNA. It is still possible to jam a NAR's buffer, but handover state is short-lived. A node sending an FBU from the NAR's link with someone else's address, or giving a wrong link-layer address, can be traced to the MN that holds the security association, much as in base Mobile IP where the PAR acts as a temporary home agent.

RtSolPr and PrRtAdv inherit the weaknesses of Neighbor Discovery, so a compromised router could point the MN at a rogue router. Where that matters, Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971) SHOULD be considered. Buffer size must be limited by local policy to avoid resource exhaustion.

HI and HAck between routers MUST be protected with security associations giving integrity and data origin authentication. The routers MUST implement IPsec (RFC 4301), and ESP in transport mode (RFC 4303) with integrity protection SHOULD be used. Confidentiality is not required. Associations can be set up manually or with IKEv2 (RFC 4306), and implementations MUST support shared secrets for mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a signature, a stranger could say 'send my friend's mail to me'. So every request must be signed, and the routers check that the new locker really belongs to the new router.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 4068 and RFC 5268
sections.content:
This protocol grew out of RFC 4068. The main addition is a security association between the MN and its access router, set up by a handover key protocol (RFC 5269 is one way). An implementation that follows this document is likely to also work with RFC 4068, except for the BADF option, which can only be processed when a security association exists. The Fast Neighbor Advertisement message is deprecated and replaced by the UNA, though a NAR may still process it as RFC 4068 describes.

Compared with RFC 5268, the change is that HI and HAck move from ICMPv6 to the Mobility Header. The RFC gives the reason: Proxy Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 both use the Mobility Header for critical signaling, so using it here lets the protocol be deployed alongside them. Subtypes 4 and 5 for the old ICMPv6 forms are deprecated and marked unavailable for future allocation.

The protocol needs no change to base Mobile IPv6, stateless address autoconfiguration or DHCP, and none to intermediate Layer 2 devices. Its one extension to Neighbor Discovery is the optional Router Advertisement sent in response to a UNA.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an updated version of older rules. The main new rule is that messages are now signed, and the messages between routers use a different envelope.

messages.label: FBU
messages.note: Binds the PCoA to the NCoA.

messages.label: FBack
messages.note: The MN then disconnects and the PAR forwards packets.

messages.label: UNA
messages.note: Sent on attaching to the NAR.

messages.label: PrRtAdv
messages.note: The MN then disconnects and connects to the NAR.

messages.label: FBU
messages.note: Forwarded through the NAR but processed only by the PAR.

messages.label: FBack and packets
messages.note: The NAR then delivers packets to the MN.

items.label: Use the tuple
items.desc: Use the supplied [AP-ID, AR-Info] tuple for movement detection and NCoA formation.

items.label: Unsolicited trigger
items.desc: Sent unsolicited; acts as a network-initiated handover trigger.

items.label: No new router info
items.desc: Each option carries an Option-Code giving the outcome.

items.label: Subset only
items.desc: Router information is present for only some of the requested access points.

items.label: Unsolicited, no trigger
items.desc: Neighbor subnet information sent unsolicited, not a handover trigger.

items.label: Use DHCP
items.desc: Perform DHCP on attaching; packets are forwarded to the PCoA.
